Q: Filling JTable with initialized columns A:

Your question was about adding rows, so why are you suddenly talking about adding columns? Abra’s approach allows adding rows without touching the column model at all. That’s what your original question was about. While it’s an entirely different question, adding columns to an existing table model when it’s basically showing properties of list elements, is also possible in simple way.

Q: Is there any way we can help Stack Overflow Website get back up? A:

I don't want to receive downvotes because auto-translation mistranslated something.

And besides, every major browser has built-in feature to automatically translate a website, why would it be needed on Stack Overflow as well?

Q: How to turn off windows integrated authentication in Chrome A:

I got this response from an internal admin and it seems to work.

I think the best we came up with was to create a shortcut to chrome.exe on your desktop and modify the target of the shortcut to be something like:

"C:\Program Files (x86)\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --auth-server-whitelist="_"

Edit: Corrected the path for misplaced backslashes. Note also the (x86), just in case.

Edit 2026: The flag was changed to: --auth-server-allowlist

"C:\Program Files (x86)\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --auth-server-allowlist="_"

Q: Runner button not showing and No tests found A:

Root cause:

  • The Excel sheet name must exactly match the name referenced in the test code.

  • If the sheet does not exist, the spec file throws an error during import.

  • Because Playwright registers tests at load time, which prevents test discovery, resulting in a missing VS Code Runner button & a "No tests found" error when running tests from the CLI.

Q: Self-recursing-iterative functions in Python A:

I am not exactly sure why you start with add(), since Knuth's up-arrow notation, in its lowest level, starts with multiplication (compare Wikipedia article).

Anyway – a naive, straightforward implementation of the definition would be:

def i(a, b, arrows):
    if arrows == 1:
        return a ** b  # Break recursion at lowest level (one arrow)
    result = a
    for _ in range(b-1):  # "-1", because we init `result` with `a`
        result = i(a, result, arrows=arrows-1)
    return result

Which we can sanity-check by some of the small results explicitly listed in the already mentioned Wikipedia article:

print(f"{i(2, 4, arrows=1)=:,}")
# i(2, 4, arrows=1)=16
print(f"{i(2, 4, arrows=2)=:,}")
# i(2, 4, arrows=2)=65,536
print(f"{i(3, 3, arrows=2)=:,}")
# i(3, 3, arrows=2)=7,625,597,484,987
print(f"{i(2, 3, arrows=3)=:,}")
# i(2, 3, arrows=3)=65,536

If you want to stay really true to the definition, you could replace a ** b by a for-loop as well, namely over multiplications. This, in turn, you could use to shorten and unify the code a bit more:

from operator import mul

def i(a, b, arrows):
    # Break recursion by explictly calling `mul()` for `arrows == 1`,
    # lower `i` by one arrow otherwise
    i_lower = mul if arrows == 1 else lambda a, b: i(a, b, arrows=arrows-1)
    result = a
    for _ in range(b-1):  # "-1", because we init result with a
        result = i_lower(a, result)
    return result
